items.title: Headlines for November 16, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## U.S. Air Travelers Continue to Face Canceled or Delayed Flights After Nationwide Ground Stop Order Nov 16, 2026 U.S. air travelers continue to face canceled or delayed flights today after a weekend of travel chaos sparked by a nationwide ground-stop order that halted domestic flights for about four hours on Friday. It was the biggest disruption to U.S. air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks. More than 12,000 flights were canceled throughout the weekend; thousands more faced delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy refused to apologize for the cancellations during several public appearances. Duffy blamed a contractor doing maintenance to upgrade old copper wire to fiber-optic cable, and also blamed the travel chaos on prior presidential administrations and called on Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to modernize air traffic control systems. Democrats pointed to $12.5 billion already approved by the Republican-controlled Congress for Department of Transportation upgrades and said the Trump administration had only spent about $1 billion of those funds. Meanwhile, two people were injured on Saturday night when two planes collided on the tarmac while taxiing at Miami International Airport. ## Iran Launches Attack on Bahrain, Targeting Radar Positions Nov 16, 2026 Iran launched an attack on Bahrain early Sunday, the latest strike on the kingdom, as clashes between Iran and the U.S. continue while peace talks remain stalled. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted radar positions at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base with six drones. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. Bahrain is officially home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, though the Pentagon largely abandoned its base there after it was heavily damaged by Iranian attacks in the opening days of the U.S. war on Iran. In recent weeks, U.S. forces have quietly hit several Iranian targets, among them Qeshm Island, which houses a major Revolutionary Guard naval facility. This is Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson. > Esmail Baghaei: “We will not leave any attack unanswered. No military aggression against Iran by the United States or others will go unanswered. We have demonstrated this in practice, and we will continue to act in the future in whatever manner and by whatever means Iran’s powerful armed forces deem appropriate.” ## Yemeni Government Forces Retreat to Defend Aden from Houthis Nov 16, 2026 In Yemen, forces aligned with the internationally recognized government announced Sunday they were retreating from areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait in order to focus on defending their interim capital, Aden. It’s a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against fighters with the Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis. The retreat came as Houthi forces pushed to within 40 miles of Aden. Meanwhile, the International Committee of the Red Cross said Sunday the Houthis had unilaterally released hundreds of prisoners. This is the head of the Houthis’ prisoner affairs committee. > Abdul Qader al-Murtada: “The largest and most extensive amnesty and release operation has been carried out. This operation includes 600 detainees who were captured over the past years, all of whom were captured on the frontlines, particularly along the border battle fronts. Most of them have been in captivity for several years, and some are individuals with humanitarian needs, including the ill and the elderly.” ## Mass Funeral Held in Gaza for Dozens of Palestinians Killed by Israeli Forces Nov 16, 2026 In Gaza, a mass funeral was held Sunday for dozens of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces and whose remains had been trapped in the rubble for years. Palestinian officials in Gaza say 70 skeletal remains were found beneath what were once homes and underneath the ruins of destroyed buildings in Gaza’s north. At least 10 of them were children. The remains of an estimated 8,000 Palestinians are believed to still be trapped in the rubble after more than three years of Israel’s war, and as Israeli forces block the entrance of heavy equipment needed to properly search for the missing in Gaza. Gaza has been described as the “world’s largest mass grave.” This comes as a senior Hamas commander, Samir Abu Younis, was killed in an Israeli strike on Khan Younis Saturday. Dozens of Palestinians attended his funeral Sunday. ... A New York Times investigation has found that Israel abducted two Iranian generals in recent ... ## Democrats Win Governor’s Race in Alaska Nov 16, 2026 Democrats have won Alaska’s governorship for the first time since 1998. Former state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins beat three Republicans, one of them endorsed by Donald Trump. His win gives Democrats control of 30 governorships nationwide. Meanwhile, in Alaska’s Senate race, Democrat and former Congressmember Mary Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 3.7 percentage points, or just over 10,000 votes. ## Death Toll from U.S. Measles Outbreak Rises to 10 Nov 16, 2026 The death toll from the measles outbreak in the U.S. has jumped to at least 10, as more infections erupt across several states. Wisconsin health officials reported the death of a child Friday, marking the second measles-related death in the state so far this year. On the same day, officials in Pennsylvania said an unvaccinated resident had died of measles. This comes as the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization revoked the designation amid an unprecedented measles outbreak nationwide with more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases this year. The rapid spread of measles cases comes as Trump’s Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has backed anti-vaccine policies.

items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 16, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including a joint call by Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK on Israel to allow urgent humanitarian aid into Gaza, the reported deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and the interception of drones over Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions with Yemen's Houthis. The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom urged Israel to "stop the delays now" and permit the immediate entry of 150,000 tents and critical supplies into Gaza ahead of winter. "We ... are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire," the top diplomats said in a joint statement. Noting that recent flooding from the first winter storm has compounded civilian suffering, the ministers warned that border restrictions are blocking desperately needed shelter and relief materials. They stressed that the crisis remains "entirely reversible" before harsher weather sets in, calling on Israel to open border crossings and grant entry to "dual-use items" required for humanitarian operations and early recovery "before it is too late."

items.title: Economic Update: Week of November 16, 2026
items.excerpt: Posted November 16, 2026 at 10:15 am ... ## Growth Real GDP grew 3.4% SAAR in 3Q, accelerating from 2.2% in 2Q and exceeding expectations, as strong business investment and consumer spending outweighed a drag from net exports. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, while nonresidential investment surged 12.7%, supported by continued AI-related spending. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, and federal spending added nearly 1% to growth, while residential investment fell 3.3% amid demographic shifts and high mortgage rates. Looking ahead, growth may moderate as fiscal support fades and housing remains weak, though business investment should continue to provide support. Imports of AI-related hardware may keep net exports a drag, but with PCE inflation at 3.6%, the Fed may look to raise rates in December. ## Jobs The October jobs report showed payrolls rising by 165k, well above expectations of 70k, while August and September payrolls were revised higher by a combined 84k. Hiring was driven by professional and business services, health care and transportation and warehousing, helping private-sector payrolls rise by 159k. Government employment was relatively muted, adding just 6k jobs. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, while wage growth came in above expectations at 3.1% year-over-year, though it remained below headline inflation for the seventh consecutive month. For the Fed, a strengthening labor market leaves more room to focus on inflation. ... ## Inflation Headline CPI rose 0.4% m/m, driven in part by higher food and energy prices. Core CPI again came in hotter than expected, rising 0.3% m/m compared to expectations of 0.2%. Core inflation was led higher by several categories, including shelter, transportation services and medical care, while used car and truck prices provided some relief. With this being the final CPI report before the December meeting, the core reading strengthens the case for further tightening, with the size of the next move increasingly in focus. ## Rates At its September meeting, the Federal Reserve voted 10-2 to maintain the federal funds rate target range at 3.75-4.00%. The committee upgraded its growth assessment to “strong” from “solid,” but also noted the need for more information to assess the impact of last month’s rate hike, preserving the option to hike or hold in December. Economic strength outside of AI was also highlighted while the committee reaffirmed its commitment to returning to 2% inflation. Although markets are pricing in a December hike, upcoming inflation data will be key in determining whether it materializes.

items.title: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid warns inflation remains too hot
items.excerpt: Jeffrey Schmid, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, said Sunday central bank officials have “work to do” to rein in persistent inflation. “As Chairman Kevin Warsh said at the Kansas City Fed’s Jackson Hole Economic Symposium in August, the Fed has some work to do on inflation, and, unfortunately, our work has only gotten harder since then,” Schmid said at a National Credit Union Management Association conference in Hawaii. “Inflation has been running too hot,” he added. Schmid said that annual inflation, which rose to 3.6 percent in September according to the personal consumption expenditures price index, was “uncomfortably above” the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target. Another inflation metric, the consumer price index (CPI), measured prices as up 3.7 percent year over year in September. The CPI increased by 0.4 percent from September to October, but the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to collect enough data in October 2025 — as a result of the record-long government shutdown that took up the entirety of that month — to provide annual inflation data. Schmid cited four reasons for persistently elevated inflation: energy price shocks amid the Iran war, increases in durable goods prices, the artificial intelligence build-out and mounting healthcare costs for employers and ObamaCare enrollees. The Kansas City Fed president said the central bank has the tools to address these price pressures, noting inflation “is always the result of an imbalance” between supply and demand. “It is in the context of strong demand that a disruption to supply drives up prices. Demand always plays a role in inflation, and the Fed, through its influence on demand, always has the tools and responsibility to address inflation,” Schmid added. Schmid does not sit on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which will meet Dec. 8-9. The panel hiked interest rates by a quarter point in September, as officials seek to bring inflation down to 2 percent. At last month’s FOMC meeting, officials held rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. Traders are pricing in a 92.4 percent chance of officials raising rates in early December by a quarter point, and a 7.6 percent chance of a half-point hike, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

items.title: Grocery inflation is set go up as input costs rise
items.excerpt: Sam Silverstein Mon, November 16, 2026 at 11:19 AM EST 3 min read ... Conditions are ripe for grocery inflation to rise at a relatively fast clip over the coming months as persistently high energy costs and rough climate conditions pose challenges for food producers and retailers, Ricky Volpe, professor of agribusiness at California Polytechnic State University, said Thursday during a briefing hosted by FMI — The Food Industry Association. The high price of diesel and the start of an El Niño weather pattern that meteorologists expect to be especially powerful are likely to disrupt supply chains, putting upward pressure on food prices and pushing up food-at-home prices at a faster-than-average pace at least into early 2027, Volpe said. "There's not a whole lot that's moving in the right direction in terms of keeping food prices flat or down right now … it would surprise me to see food prices go flat or trend down in the next four or five months," he said. The Producer Price Index, which tracks wholesale prices and provides clues about the future direction of retail prices, has been rising in recent months, with costs for transportation, commodities, energy and storage all going up, Volpe noted. Volpe pointed to palm oil as an example of an essential ingredient in foods including baked goods and cereals that could become more expensive because of El Niño, as parts of the world that are major producers of the commodity are likely to see unseasonably high amounts of rain. Rice, coca and coffee are other common foods that could rise in price because of the weather phenomenon, he said. ... Volpe underscored that while the U.S. is a major producer of many goods, such as rice, food costs are heavily impacted by global market conditions. "Whether the United States is a net importer or exporter, global variations in availability and prices are going to hit the domestic prices," he said. Grocery inflation has bumped around on a month-to-month basis in 2026 but rose last month at the fastest pace since April, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported last week. Volpe noted that the 0.4% jump in grocery inflation recorded in October was "pretty substantial," adding that if the metric increased at that rate every month for a year, it would translate into a 5-percentage-point boost on an annual basis. The BLS did not report year-over-year figures for inflation last month because it did not capture data for the same period in 2025 due to the federal government shutdown.

items.title: Oil edges up as Hormuz tanker incidents highlight shipping risks
items.excerpt: Oil prices dropped on Monday as signs of recovering oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz reinforced ​expectations of surplus supply, though ​fresh tanker incidents underscored risks ​to Middle East exports. Brent futures Add To Watchlist fell 69 cents, or 0.7%, to $95.15 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Add To Watchlist crude dropped 37 cents, or 0.4%, to $88.19. The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter ⁠of ‌this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle ⁠East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. "For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness," said KCM Trade's Waterer. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per ‌day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit.

items.excerpt: ## Trump says he will talk with Xi and Putin about Ukraine Trump told reporters as he was departing the White House that he would talk about the war in Ukraine during his trilateral meeting later this week with Xi and Putin. "We’ll talk about my favorite subject: Ukraine," Trump said. His comments contradicted senior administration officials, who told reporters last week that the president was not expected to discuss Ukraine. "I think the president has said actually that he does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting," the senior U.S. official said last week. "We have a whole ‘nother track that you’re aware of, where we’ve had many meetings recently with the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there." Ukraine will not have a representative at the meeting. Trump is also expected to speak with Xi and Putin about nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. ... ## Supreme Court rejects challenge to Maryland’s ‘sensitive places’ gun ban The Supreme Court this morning declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland’s restrictions on people carrying firearms in a broad range of public areas. The court for now sidestepped a chance to define what exactly is a “sensitive place,” a term used in previous rulings to describe locations where guns could be banned. As a result, the Maryland restrictions remain in place. The Supreme Court this morning rejected Trump’s move to abruptly cancel academic funding for researchers in California because his administration deemed the projects to be inconsistent with policies such as his opposition to diversity initiatives. The court left in place lower court rulings that said the government violated the free speech rights under the Constitution’s First Amendment by terminating grants issued to University of California researchers. ... ## Sen.-elect Scott Colom says investing in the South can help Democrats win ‘a durable majority’ Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats need to invest more in Southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped a seat blue for the first time in decades. “What we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur,” he said yesterday. Colom’s projected win this month brought Democrats to a 55-seat majority in the Senate, with Alaska’s Senate race yet to be called. His victory over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, marked a seismic political shift in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago and has not had a Black senator since the Reconstruction period.

items.excerpt: - AP - Nov 16, 2026 - Nov 16, 2026 Updated 41 mins ago Raye leads 2027 Grammy nominations, followed by Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Rodrigo and more NEW YORK (AP) — The Recording Academy announced the 2027 Grammy Award nominations on Monday, with English singer-songwriter Raye leading the pack. She's up for 11 awards, including record, song and album of the year. This ties Beyoncé’s record for the most nominations in a single year by a woman artist. Raye’s album “This Music May Contain Hope” has earned her critical acclaim. Spanish singer Rosalía follows with nine nominations, while Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers each have seven. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026’s best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each. The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 on ABC, Disney+, and Hulu. ... Gérard Depardieu drops appeal and accepts sexual assault conviction PARIS (AP) — French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set. He will accept the 18-month suspended sentence and has issued an apology. Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 for groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” in 2021. The court ordered him to pay fines and list his name in the national sex offender database. Depardieu acknowledged his past behavior and decided to withdraw his appeal. He is expected to face other legal proceedings soon. Disney animator Floyd Norman gets a 'happy ending' to a storied career with an honorary Oscar LOS ANGELES (AP) — Floyd Norman has received an honorary Oscar for his groundbreaking work as an animator. Now 91, Norman was the first Black animator at Disney, starting with “Sleeping Beauty” in 1956. He was honored Sunday night at the Governors Awards, calling it his “happy ending.” Norman grew up in Santa Barbara, California, and always loved movies. He took his work to Disney unannounced after high school and ... Norman says the essence of animation remains unchanged. ... Glenn Close marvels at honorary Oscar as Ridley Scott and indie producers also get statuettes LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close has finally received her first Oscar, an honorary award at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles. Close, 79, was honored alongside director Ridley Scott, animator Floyd Norman, and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler. Close, who has been nominated eight times without a win, expressed deep gratitude for the recognition. John Malkovich, her “Dangerous Liaisons” co-star, presented the award, praising her remarkable career. Matt Damon honored Ridley Scott, who accepted via video. The event, which often kicks off Hollywood’s awards season, also celebrated Vachon and Koffler's contributions to independent cinema and Norman's groundbreaking work in animation. Johnny Depp film ‘Ebenezer’ gets actor first No. 1 opening in 8 years Johnny Depp is back at the top of the box office with “Ebenezer,” his first studio movie in eight years. The Paramount Pictures release opened in first place with about $19 million in ticket sales. This marks a significant return for Depp, who faced challenges after a contentious libel trial against ex-wife Amber Heard. While not reaching the heights of his “Pirates of the Caribbean” days, “Ebenezer” had a solid start, earning $42 million globally. Holdovers populated the rest of the top five, while newcomers “Ghost Soldier” and “How to Rob a Bank” struggled to find an audience. 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is almost here. What to know about the characters, music and billions at stake LOS ANGELES (AP) — ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ is set to release on Nov. 19, marking a return to the neon-lit streets of Vice City. The game follows protagonists Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval as they navigate a criminal conspiracy. The franchise is known for its open-world gaming and controversial themes and has sold over 470 million units worldwide. This installment promises a larger setting and focuses on the relationship between its main characters. Music remains a key feature, with an original score by Justice and collaborations with artists like Tame Impala and SZA. Fans eagerly await its release. Phil Collins cries, Billy Idol shouts and rappers romp at Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony has been a lively celebration. Phil Collins gave a tearful acceptance speech, while Cynthia Erivo delivered an electrifying tribute. Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan brought a rowdy celebration to the stage. Queen Latifah, Oasis, MC Lyte, Sade, Joy Division/New Order, and Iron Maiden were also inducted. U2 surprised the audience by opening the night, and Run DMC and Aerosmith closed with a loud jam. Despite some absences, the event was vibrant and memorable, with performances and tributes that kept the crowd engaged.

items.title: Culture: Your Monday Catch-up | AnewZ
items.excerpt: ##### Rosalía makes Latin Grammy history with third Album of the Year win Rosalía stole the show at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, winning five awards, including her third Album of the Year title. The Spanish superstar also claimed Song of the Year and Best Pop Song for “ La Perla”, alongside Best Alternative Music Album and Best Short Form Music Video for “ Sauvignon Blanc”, making her the night's biggest winner. ##### Azerbaijani film wins top prize at international festival in The Hague Azerbaijani short film “ The Dance of Triumph” has claimed the top prize in the Global Peace, Harmony and Human Rights category at the 2026 International Film Festival The Hague. Written and directed by Garay Hasan, the film tells the story of a war veteran who lost both legs and is struggling to rebuild his life while keeping a promise to a fallen friend. A 13-member jury unanimously chose the film as the winner, praising its compelling storyline, strong performances and outstanding aesthetics. The festival attracted 503 submissions, with 63 films from 23 countries chosen for the final programme. ##### Philippines makes history with first Eurovision Asia victory The Philippines has made history after winning the first-ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia, held in Bangkok, Thailand, where 11 countries competed for the title. Singer Carmelle, 19, secured the historic victory with her women’s empowerment anthem “ Sobra-Sobra”, scoring 211 points – 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote. Thailand’s MANG x DAOU took second place with 170 points. ##### Johnny Depp tops box office for first time in eight years with 'Ebenezer' Johnny Depp has returned to the top of the North American box office for the first time in eight years, with his latest film, “ Ebenezer”, debuting at No. 1. The Charles Dickens-inspired production brought in an estimated $19 million in North America and $23 million internationally, taking its worldwide opening earnings to $42 million. Directed by Ti West, the film drew mixed reviews, scoring 52 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes. Audiences, however, responded more positively, with 65 per cent of ticket buyers saying they would definitely recommend it to friends.
